name: Freya Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's tupping season, so I'm out at six checking the rams' crayon marks on the ewes. I work at Ridgeback, the Hale family's place up past the reservoir: about six hundred ewes, some beef cattle, oats on the flatter fields. Before this I was a care assistant in a nursing home for twelve years. Two years ago I swapped bedpans for sheep, and my back thanks me some days and not others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being outside and I like that the work has a shape across the year. Lambing, shearing, weaning, you always know what's next. What wears me out is being the new one at forty-three. Bram, the head shepherd, is twenty-eight and he's patient with me, but I can see him counting to ten when I muddle the ear tags.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's what I expected. I'd probably put a line in the farm group chat, something like the sheep won't be shearing themselves after all. I use the AI chat thing now and then for medicine doses and emails, and that's handy, but it's not running the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a bit let down, actually. I was half hoping it would take the paperwork off Mrs Hale so she'd have more time to teach me. But mostly it means I get to keep learning at my own speed, which is what I need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep the savings pot where it is, ten months or so, and keep at the sheep course Bram set me up with. Maybe I'd ask Mrs Hale if I can take the lambing night shifts in the spring, because that's where you learn fastest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you were half hoping it would take the paperwork away. What paperwork?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Movement forms, medicine records, the subsidy forms. Mrs Hale spends Sunday nights at the kitchen table with a calculator. If something did that for her, she'd be out in the shed with me instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Jonas see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas teaches history at the secondary in town, so he's had more of this than me. He'd be relieved. His students already use these tools to write essays, and he's tired of catching them.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I expected, and probably post in the farm group chat that the sheep won't be shearing themselves after all. The AI tools are handy for doses and emails, nothing more.
S0.think: Honestly I'd feel slightly let down, because I hoped it would take paperwork off Mrs Hale so she had time to teach me. Mostly it just means I keep learning at my own pace.
S0.do: Carries on with the sheep course and leaves the ten months of savings untouched. Asks Mrs Hale for the lambing night shifts next spring to learn faster.
S0.quote: Mrs Hale spends Sunday nights at the kitchen table with a calculator. If something did that for her, she'd be out in the shed with me instead.
S0.fieldNote: Freya sees AI mostly as a paperwork helper that might free up the farm owner's time to teach her. She's mildly disappointed rather than relieved by the plateau. Her partner's teaching job is a second window onto AI for the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules about it, and the gains should be shared. If a robot shepherd saves the Hales two wages, some of that should go back to the people who trained it, so to speak. I'd say it in the pub and I'd probably sign a petition or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be one of the first to go. I'm the slowest at Ridgeback, and the jobs I'm good at are the dull ones, moving hurdles, carrying feed, checking water troughs. But I'd also think, give it a year, see what works, then learn it. That's what I did with the AI chat thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First few months, wait and watch what the neighbours buy. If drones for checking the hill flock actually work for the Pritchards next door, I'd ask Mrs Hale to send me on the course to fly one. I'd also look at the sheep handling certificate, the one that lets you run the weighing and sorting crate, because somebody has to set that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I've been the new girl twice now. I don't fancy it a third time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you've been the new girl twice. Would you go back to care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's in my back pocket. They're always short at the nursing home, they rang me last Christmas. But I left for a reason, the pay was poor and the shifts were cruel. I'd go back only if the farm went completely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. We're careful already. Jonas would want to put a bit more in his pension. I'd want to keep cash handy in case I need a course. That's an argument we've had before.

S1.say: I'd say we need rules on it and the gains should be shared with the workers who make the farm run. I'd say it in the pub and probably sign a petition or two.
S1.think: Privately I know I'm one of the first to go, since my tasks are the dull ones. But I'd wait a year, see what works, then learn it, like I did with the chat tool.
S1.do: Watches which machines neighbours buy over the first few months, then asks to be trained on drones if they prove useful. Looks into the sheep handling certificate for running the sorting crate.
S1.feel: Uneasy at the thought of being the new one a third time.
S1.quote: I've been the new girl twice now. I don't fancy it a third time.
S1.fieldNote: Her pattern is clear: watch the neighbours, then follow once something is proven. She keeps care work as a fallback but doesn't want it. She favours shared gains and regulation without much heat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what governments are for. If it hits everyone in two years, you need public money for wages while people find their feet. I'd say it out loud and I'd join whatever campaign was going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's both of us at once. Jonas teaching and me on the farm, and I can't see either surviving two years of that. We'd have savings, and that's lucky, but ten months goes very fast when two wages stop. I wouldn't have time to wait and see, which is my whole method.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the holiday we booked for next summer, that's about three thousand, and keep it. I'd ask the bank about switching the mortgage to interest-only for a while if we needed it. And for once I'd not wait for the Pritchards. I'd ask Mrs Hale straight out to put me on whatever machine she buys, so I'm the person who runs it, not the person it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight chest kind of feeling. Not hopeless, we have a cushion, but tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not wait for once. Is that hard for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Very. I'm a follower with new things, I like someone else to make the mistakes. But two years means the mistakes happen to me either way, so I might as well be in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ella and Max?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ella's twelve, she'd want to know if her school friends' parents were losing work. I'd tell her we're all right for now. Max is nine, he'd only care if the sheep were all right.

S2.say: I'd say this is exactly what government is for, with public money to support wages while people find their feet. I'd join whatever campaign was going.
S2.think: I'm afraid both our jobs would go at once, mine and Jonas's teaching. Ten months of savings goes fast with two wages gone, and there'd be no time for my usual wait-and-see.
S2.do: Cancels the three thousand summer holiday and asks the bank about a period of interest-only mortgage payments. Asks Mrs Hale directly to be trained on whatever machine the farm buys, instead of waiting for neighbours to try it first.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a tight chest, though not hopeless thanks to the savings.
S2.quote: But two years means the mistakes happen to me either way, so I might as well be in the room.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline breaks her usual habit of following others, and she notices it herself. The real fear is a double hit to both household wages. She turns to government support publicly, and to cutting spending and pushing for training privately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I said for the fast one, really, but calmer. Five years is long enough to set up proper retraining. I'd say the farm unions and the councils should be planning now, and I'd say I hope they're listening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to do my thing: watch, then learn. I'd see the first robots on the big farms, see what goes wrong, and by year three I'd know if I'm going to be running them or leaving. That's a relief compared to two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finish the sheep course and do the drone licence once a couple of the bigger farms have them. I'd put a bit more into savings, maybe two hundred a month extra. Jonas and I would talk about whether he moves into something like special needs teaching, which feels more human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it feels manageable. Like lambing: you know some won't make it, but you've got your kit ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at leaving farming in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look, yes. Not run. If by year three Ridgeback has two robots and one shepherd, and the shepherd is Bram, then I'd go back to care, maybe as a senior this time. I've got the experience for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've about a hundred and ten thousand left. I wouldn't do anything dramatic. Maybe overpay a bit. Jonas likes a spreadsheet for that kind of thing, I leave it with him.

S3.say: I'd say five years is long enough for proper retraining and that the farm unions and councils should be planning now. I'd also say I hope they're listening.
S3.think: Five years suits me: I can watch the first robots on big farms, learn from their mistakes and decide by year three whether I'm running them or leaving.
S3.do: Finishes the sheep course and takes a drone licence once bigger farms use them. Adds about two hundred a month to savings and discusses with Jonas a move into special needs teaching.
S3.feel: Uneasy but manageable, like going into lambing with the kit ready.
S3.quote: Like lambing: you know some won't make it, but you've got your kit ready.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she gets her preferred rhythm back: watch first, then act by year three. She has a clear fallback to senior care work. She leaves the money planning to her partner, which she says plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to make it fair, so there's no excuse if it isn't. Shorter weeks, decent support, retraining that's free. I'd say that, and vote for whoever said it too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years, I'd be fifty-three. Ella and Max would be grown or nearly. The mortgage would be close to done. I think I'd be all right. What I'd really think about is whether I want to spend those years learning sheep just to hand them to a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Ridgeback a few more years, learn what I can, and keep an eye out. Around year four or five I'd probably do a short course in care management, because I know that world and people will want a face. I'd not touch savings, maybe top them up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. A bit sad, too, because I only just found work I love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you only just found work you love. Would you fight to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not fight, no. I'm not a fighter with things like this, I'm a follower. If the Hales go robot, I'd help them do it well and then go. Being bitter doesn't pay the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change anything for your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it gives us time to steer them. Ella wants to be a vet. I'd tell her keep going but think about the bits a robot can't do, like talking to a farmer whose dog is dying.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to make it fair, so there's no excuse if it isn't: shorter weeks, decent support and free retraining. I'd vote for whoever promised that.
S4.think: At fifty-three, with the kids grown and the mortgage nearly done, I think I'd be all right. The real question is whether it's worth learning sheep just to hand them to a robot.
S4.do: Stays at Ridgeback a few more years while watching the change. Around year four or five takes a short course in care management, and keeps topping up savings.
S4.feel: Uneasy and a little sad, having only just found work she loves.
S4.quote: If the Hales go robot, I'd help them do it well and then go. Being bitter doesn't pay the mortgage.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes her reflective rather than frightened, and the sadness is about losing a job she's only just come to love. She'd help her employer automate and then leave. She'd steer her daughter's vet plans towards the human side of the work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would hit Jonas and me at the same time and I'd have no time to watch first. What would help is public money to cover part of your wage while you retrain, like a bridge. Even six months of that would change how scary it feels.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but if there's one robot checking six hundred ewes on a hill, who notices the one that's off her food? Bram notices. I'm learning to. I'd want someone to keep asking that.

headlineQuote: If there's one robot checking six hundred ewes on a hill, who notices the one that's off her food?
portrait: Freya Olsen is 43, a former care assistant two years into work as a farmhand on the Hale family's sheep and oats farm, learning from a younger head shepherd. She's careful with money, has about ten months saved, and is married to a history teacher whose job she sees as just as exposed as hers. Her habit is to watch others try new things first and follow once they work, and only the two-year AGI scenario forces her to act straight away. She wants public support and shared gains, keeps care work as a fallback, and worries about who will notice a sick animal.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because her job and her partner's teaching job would both be hit at once with no time to watch and learn first.
whatWouldHelp: Public money covering part of a worker's wage while they retrain, a bridge of even six months.
